content:
What happens when accountability becomes optional for people deemed “too valuable” to lose? We may have just found out with the latest Nvidia news.

For most employees, violating a company ethics policy — let alone compromising sensitive information — ends with a permanent exit and no second act. At the top of the corporate ladder, however, the rules operate differently.

Nvidia announced Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as its chief executive officer on Monday, days after President Donald Trump advocated for his return on social media. Nvidia’s interim CEO and CFO, Colette Kress, and other top executives were reportedly excluded from the board’s meeting with Trump to discuss the decision on Sunday afternoon, Bloomberg reported.

Huang’s reinstatement comes less than two weeks after he resigned following reports of two extramarital affairs, including with Alice Huang, who was thought to have been a Chinese asset. U.S. intelligence is said to have found evidence Alice was connected with an official at China’s top spy agency for over a year when she was involved with Huang, The New York Times reported before news broke that Huang was reinstated.

The president spoke to CNBC after the news broke, telling them he “convinced” Nvidia to make the decision: “I made the deal.” He said he reassured the board that Huang would not be considered a threat to national security and told CNBC Huang “did nothing wrong.”

“I’ve seen some unbelievably talented CEOs get thrown out because they were kissing somebody inappropriately at a game or something,” Trump said. “They never got somebody back who was as good.”

“People say, is it a threat to have him? No, it’s a threat to lose him,” Trump continued. “I’m very, very happy that the company had the courage and the board had the courage to do the right thing. And they suffered for two weeks, and the company suffered greatly.”

Trump went on to argue, “Sex sells.”

The news was released before the stock market opened on Monday, and Nvidia’s share price went up about 30% by the afternoon. When asked about the administration’s involvement in Nvidia reinstating Huang, the White House referred HuffPost to Trump’s CNBC interview, in which Trump said he had spoken about Huang with President Xi Jinping when he visited China last week to meet with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Huang, who said in a Nov. 17 statement that he had made “serious mistakes” but hoped to return, has not commented publicly since his reinstatement, as of publication.

While Trump is celebrating by posting wildly inappropriate memes, lawmakers on both sides expressed concern and confusion over the decision’s ethics. Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) asked on X whether the FBI had given Huang a defensive briefing and whether he ignored warnings, while Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) wrote, “The President is selling out our national security to keep the stock market high.”

Huang is still expected to testify before the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence and China Select committees on Dec. 1. Nvidia did not respond to HuffPost’s request for comment.

Beneath the political and market drama sits a concern that hits close to home for a lot of everyday Americans: Do ethical standards only apply to people who don’t move the S&P 500?

Excusing Huang’s behavior to protect Nvidia stock doesn’t just bend the rules at the top, but erodes trust everywhere below it, said Charles Elson, the founding director of the University of Delaware’s Weinberg Center for Corporate Governance.

“The market’s reaction is short term,” Elson said. “Markets move up and down, but ultimately the value of the company is determined by the success of its leadership and its board.”

When it comes to the disruption over the past two weeks, Elson put the blame on Huang.

“It’s [Huang’s] fault. It’s not the public’s. It’s him. He should be held accountable,” Elson said. “If he didn’t do this, it would have never happened.”

Elson said he could not recall another president weighing in to rehabilitate a disgraced executive who had been removed.

“That makes no sense,” he told HuffPost. “That’s not his wheelhouse. I think he’s wrong. I mean, he stepped out of his lane, so to speak. It shows weakness on the part of the board.”

Why ‘Geniuses’ Often Get A Pass

Elson compares Huang’s reinstatement with what he calls Silicon Valley’s “genius theory”: the idea that ordinary rules and ethics do not apply to people considered “geniuses,” because a genius should be allowed to do what they want so society will be better in the end.

“To suggest that for some reason, because of someone’s talents, that they are not expected to comport themselves as reasonable people in a free and organized society is just wrong,” Elson said. “It leads to all kinds of problems.”

To Elson, that double standard is absurd on its face. “Does that mean that the law of driving, speeding is not applicable?” he asked. “Does it mean that you don’t have to get a driver’s license because you’re so talented?”

Problems will likely arise within Nvidia and other companies as a result, Elson argued.

“It either means people will start doing it [themselves], which is bad for the company, or, better yet, that they are demoralized because [Huang is] held to a different standard than they are,” Elson said. “If [any company’s] board or its leadership has demonstrated significant lack of judgment or created an environment where folks do not believe in the organization [or] that appropriate conduct is respected, the company will never succeed long term.”

What Jensen Huang’s Reinstatement Signals To The Rest Of Us

Alison Taylor, a business ethics professor at New York University and author of “Higher Ground,” told HuffPost that personal relationships in the workplace violate standard codes of conduct, yet double standards persist.

“A regular person is going to be like, ‘If that was me, I would be fired on the spot, no question,’” Taylor said.

For Taylor, the board’s decision to rush through the reversal without a thorough review or investigation carries major risks beyond a market reaction.

“There’s the risk of, we now have this company that stands or falls by Trump’s decisions,” she said. “Instead, they don’t even give it [10] days. They don’t even let [an investigation finish]. They don’t even try to make this look like anything other than it is.”

For Nvidia employees specifically, the immediate response could be that they’re relieved since a lot of them are dependent on the stock. But over time, regular employees will begin to register that the rules only apply to them and they are replaceable, while top leaders are untouchable.

“You’re replaceable, you don’t have a job. You don’t have a pension, you don’t have a future,” she said. “But, you know, apparently the person … [who is] making all this happen isn’t replaceable.”

“[The situation] massively juices all that discourse about unaccountable billionaires that think they’re above the law and the corruption,” she added, warning that there is likely “a slow drip of negative, strange, lack of good judgment” stories tied to Nvidia that will come out.
